scenes.title: Cold open
narration: After a century-long ban by missionaries who labeled it 'devil's frolic,' Yup'ik dance was revived in the 1980s, restoring the drum as the central pulse of the community.
This is Yup'ik dance. Ancient to present (revived 1980s).
on_screen: Title card: Yup'ik dance · United States (Alaska) · Ancient to present (revived 1980s)

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated as a communal activity in the qasgiq (community center) for ceremonies and festivals.
In the late 19th century, Christian missionaries banned the practice, labeling it 'heathen idol worship' and 'black art.' Russian Orthodox priests forbade village dance feasts as late as 1933.
The tradition saw a major revival starting in 1982 at St. Mary's to ensure the survival of cultural heritage.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Dance is the heart of spiritual life, used to request survival needs, tell stories, or ridicule individuals through affectionate teasing.
Specific festivals include the Messenger Feast (kevgiq) and the Bladder Festival (nakaciuq).
It embodies the Yup'ik conception of the world and the connection between animals and spirits.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: College Gate Yup'ik Immersion Yuraq Dancers 2024 Education Center Holiday Performance (https://archive.org/details/asdk12ak-College_Gate_Yup_ik_Immersion_Yuraq_Dancers_2024_Education_Center_Holiday_Performance)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance follows a specific cultural format: men are typically in the front kneeling, while women stand in the back.
Dancers use hand-held fans (tegumiaq) made of woven grass or wooden hoops with feathers to accentuate fluid arm movements.
Rhythmic gestures are combined with storytelling and song.
Watch for Cauyarialnguq, Pamyua.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Linear rows with men in front and women behind; drummers at the very back.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The drum (cauyaq) is the only instrument used.
It consists of a round bentwood frame with a handle, traditionally covered with mammal stomach lining.
Listen for the Cauyaq (bentwood frame drum), Cauyaun (drum stick).
The sound is dominated by the resonant, sharp strike of a single or multiple frame drums hit from above, accompanying unison or melodic chanting in the Yup'ik language.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Regalia includes the qaspeq (calico pullover), qaliq (fancy fur parka), nasqurrun (beaded headdress), and piluguuk (decorated boots).
Men use wooden fans with waterfowl or owl feathers, while women use woven grass or caribou fans.
Historically performed in the qasgiq, it is now performed at festivals and community centers.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Shamans (angalkut) were the primary leaders and mask-carvers who mediated with the spirit world.
Contemporary revival efforts were led by artists and elders in Negeqliq (St. Mary's) in 1982 to pass traditions to the youth.
Variants include Cup'ik dance (Chevak dialect) and Cup'ig dance (Nunivak Island).
The tradition is passed down through family lines, especially 'yurapiaq' (real dance) sequences which may be owned by individuals.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Yup'ik dance is sibling of Iñupiaq dance: Differs in drum technique (struck from below) and male posture (standing).

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Masked dances (nepcetat) represent powerful spirits and were historically mediated by shamans; some rituals are restricted or no longer practiced due to their high spiritual content.

scenes.title: Until next time
narration: Witness the rebirth of a forbidden tradition as the Yup'ik people reclaim their spiritual heritage through the pulse of the cauyaq.
